title: POC Weekly Sync - Reliability Incident Follow-up
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on the March 24 reliability incident. We reviewed findings: transient 5xxs tied to request bursts hitting rate-limit/fallback, retry storms from client-side SDK, and a KV cache miss surge after canary. Agreed next steps: run extended load tests with Priya to reproduce, implement rate-limit headers and backoff guidance, tweak batching/quantization profiles, and run a focused end-to-end test with customer traffic patterns. Security and logging gaps (missing structured request IDs in some traces) to be fixed before next check-in.

5xx patterns vs timeouts and connection drops
KV/prefix cache misses after canary deploy
Observability gaps: request IDs, per-route tracing
Next steps: load tests, docs/SDK backoff guidance, follow-up benchmark

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Sam Rivera (Acme CTO), Lina Chen (Acme SRE), Marcus Bell (Acme Product)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be incomplete): Follow-up to yesterday's incident. Main workstreams: reproduce, fix client backoff guidance, improve tracing.

[00:00] Jordan: ok hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick check on audio, can you hear me?
[00:05] Sam: yep good here, loud and clear
[00:08] Jordan: cool. this is the weekly poc sync, main focus is the incident from March 24 where you saw a series of 5xx spikes and timeouts. Priya and I will walk through the logs and proposed mitigations, then we'll align on next steps.
[00:25] Priya: thanks. quick note, I've got the canary traces pulled, and there are a couple of interesting patterns: brief burst at 15:42 UTC where rate limiting kicked in, then a client retry wave that amplified traffic. also saw a KV cache miss surge right after the canary patch, looks like prefix cache keys weren't warmed.
[00:45] Lina: yeah that matches what we saw, our side logged repeated 429s then a bunch of retries which turned into 5xxs on some of the downstream endpoints. the retry TTLs weren't exponential in our SDK, so it was basically retrying too aggressively.
[01:02] Marcus: can you explain, like, when you say KV cache miss, is that the prefix cache in Redwood or our own caching layer?
[01:08] Priya: good question. this is Redwood's prefix/K-V cache — the front-end would normally hit a cached K V entry for session prefixes to avoid a full model compute. after the canary, the cache keys were slightly different due to a small tokenize change, so miss rate spiked. that increased per-request compute and caused more long-running requests.
[01:30] Sam: ah, tokenizer change, okay that makes sense. any idea why that was rolled without warming?
[01:36] Jordan: sequence of events — small tokenizer tweak in canary, the config didn't include the warmup job, and because we route some traffic to canary early, it caused a brief period of higher tail latency. we should have rollback signals, we do, but the retry and rate limit interaction made it worse.
[01:55] Lina: another factor: some of our client-side timeouts are quite short, so when we saw a timeout the client retried immediately with default retry policy. we need better guidance in the SDK.
[02:10] Priya: totally, we can push an SDK note and a recommended backoff algorithm example. also we can return more explicit rate-limit headers so clients can back off better — right now some clients treat 5xx as retryable without considering Retry-After or rate-limit remaining headers.
[02:30] Marcus: do you have a recommended retry budget? like for our product flows what's safe?
[02:34] Priya: it depends on the latency budget. for sub-second interactive flows, keep retries to 1 with exponential backoff starting at 200ms; for async batch jobs you can allow more aggressive retries. we'll put concrete numbers in the doc.
[02:52] Jordan: also, on the server side, we can enforce per-customer burst limits and smoother throttling to avoid hammering due to client retries. but that requires coordination if you want no failed calls in peak windows.
[03:06] Sam: from a product perspective, we need to know impact to user experience — how long did tail latencies last?
[03:12] Priya: tail spiked for about 7 minutes, with 95th around 1.8s and some p99s near 6s when cache misses were high. we have the raw traces, will share.
[03:26] Jordan: note that some p99s resulted in HTTP 504 or 502, not all 5xx are the same, some were timeouts at the gateway layer.
[03:36] Lina: on logging, we noticed missing structured request IDs in a subset of traces — makes correlating client->server harder. can we add guaranteed request-id propagation?
[03:45] Priya: yes we can instrument forced request-id header propagation and include it in all logs and traces; we'll update the debug snapshot.
[03:55] Marcus: any security or compliance impacts? customers always ask about logs and PII.
[03:59] Jordan: nothing affecting data residency or encryption. we did see some unredacted debug fields in ephemeral logs during the incident; we'll scrub those and follow SOC 2 log retention guidance. we will also double check KMS key access audit for the time window.
[04:16] Sam: ok good. what's the plan to reproduce this?
[04:20] Priya: we'll run a 48-hour load test mimicking your burst pattern, include tokenization mismatch scenarios to trigger cache misses, and vary client retry configs to find the sweet spot. I'll attach the test harness and results.
[04:33] Jordan: we'll also run a canary with warmup step so we can measure the difference and validate rollout safety.
[04:40] Lina: do you have a mitigations doc — in the short term can we add rate-limit headers so our SDK can respect Retry-After?
[04:47] Priya: yes, we'll add explicit X-RateLimit-Remaining and Retry-After headers and return 429s more deterministically when we're hitting capacity. also add 503 with Retry-After for transient maintenance.
[05:01] Sam: and the SDK change — timeline?
[05:04] Jordan: we'll draft an SDK guidance doc tonight, Priya will share examples by Friday.
[05:12] Priya: quick aside, we've seen some naming mismatches in traces — e.g., 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cache' in auto logs, so watch for that when searching.
[05:22] (laughter)
[05:25] Marcus: are there any planned changes to batching or quantization that could affect latency? we tested quantize-8 last week, did that matter?
[05:33] Priya: quantization affects cost/latency tradeoffs; the incident was primarily cache/keying+retries not quantization. but we will include a recommended batching config for your traffic to reduce per-token overhead.
[05:46] Jordan: ok let's capture concrete next steps. Priya will run the 48-hour test and share logs, Lina sends sample traffic and client configs, Jordan shares canary diffs and debug snapshot. we'll then schedule a joint replay on a dedicated pool to validate fixes. any objections?
[06:05] Sam: sounds good. one ask: can we get an SLA addendum scenario for POC month if this repeats?
[06:11] Jordan: we can draft a temporary SLA or a runbook for incident handling, yes. we'll share options.
[06:18] Lina: also can we add more trace retention for the window of the POC? helps debugging.
[06:22] Priya: we can bump retention for the POC to 30 days for debug traces, will flag cost implications.
[06:29] Marcus: ok thanks.
[06:31] Jordan: I'll recap in the follow-up email and attach the debug snapshot + logs.
[06:35] Sam: thanks everyone.
[06:38] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: speaker labels are sometimes approximate; filler words and overlaps preserved. Links referenced: deployment diffs (internal link), debug snapshot (shared drive), SDK guidance draft (to be attached).
